narrative:
The model estimated a 51.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than not—and that narrow prediction led to denial. This is not a certainty; it means the model saw your profile as just on the failing side of the line.

The strongest reason was your third-year class rank. You were in the first decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile among accepted students, and this was the most influential factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and, despite being slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37, it pushed toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA was third in importance; at 3.40, above the accepted average of about 3.23, it also pushed toward passing. Overall, those positive academic signals were outweighed by the very low third-year rank.

To strengthen a future application, ask admissions for feedback, focus on demonstrating improved advanced academic performance, and consider whether retaking the LSAT or adding coursework that shows readiness for law study would help. You should also build a clear bar-exam preparation plan and reapply when your record more convincingly shows you can succeed.
